title: Random forests
objectives: Decorrelate the trees by choosing features at random.
Explain why only lower correlation, not more trees, lowers the variance floor of an average.

screens.title: Every tree starts the same way
screens.prose: We bag 100 deep trees on 400 loans, as in lesson 5. Each tree may split on any of the 8 features. Here are the root splits of the first six, beside a forest that we will explain shortly.

state.caption: The first 6 of 100 trees grown on the same 400 loans (book 9). All 100 bagged trees start with leverage.

screens.question: Every bagged tree opens with leverage. What does that do to their vote?

options.text: The trees make similar mistakes, so averaging them cancels less
Nothing bad: leverage is the best feature, so it belongs at every root
options.why: Leverage is the best single split, yes. But 100 trees that agree at the root share their errors, and shared errors do not average away.

options.text: The trees are identical, so the vote equals one tree
options.why: The thresholds differ, from −0.57 to 0.40, and the lower splits differ more. The trees are alike, not identical.

options.text: It does not matter, because the deeper splits differ anyway
options.why: The root decides which half of the book each subtree sees. Trees that share it stay alike all the way down.

hints.text: Recall the fifty analysts who read the same filings.
Compare the two columns: how many different root features does each use?
Trees that agree at the root tend to be wrong on the same loans. Correlated errors do not cancel.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens to an average when its parts move together.

explain.text: Bagged trees all split first on leverage, so they send loans down similar paths and err on similar loans. Their errors are correlated, which is why the lesson 5 curve flattened so early. The right-hand column shows a forest that breaks the habit.

screens.title: Correlation sets a floor
screens.prose: Each tree's prediction has variance $\sigma^2$, and any two trees have correlation $\rho$. The curve shows the variance of the average of $B$ trees. Slide $\rho$ and watch where the curve ends.

params.yLabel: Variance of the average, in units of $\sigma^2$

screens.question: With $\rho = 0.5$, what value does the variance approach as $B$ grows, in units of $\sigma^2$?

widget.label: Limit of the variance, in units of sigma squared

hints.text: Slide $\rho$ to 0.5 and read the right end of the curve.
Try $\rho = 0$ and $\rho = 1$ too: where does the curve end each time?
The curve flattens at $\rho$ itself: 0 for independent trees, 1 for identical ones.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $\rho$ to 0.5 and watch what the curve levels off at.

byKey.zero: That is the independent case, $\rho = 0$. With $\rho = 0.5$ the curve stops at a floor.
byKey.b100: 0.505 is the value at $B = 100$. As $B$ keeps growing it settles a little lower, at 0.5.
byKey.one: 1 is where the curve starts, at $B = 1$.

explain.text: At $\rho = 0$ the curve falls like $1/B$ towards 0. At $\rho = 0.5$ it levels off at half of $\sigma^2$, and at $\rho = 1$ it never falls. More trees cannot get below the floor $\rho\sigma^2$.

screens.title: Where the floor comes from
screens.prose: Let $X_1, \dots, X_B$ be the trees' predictions for one loan, each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$, so each covariance is $\rho\sigma^2$. Derive the curve you just slid.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_b X_b\right) = \frac{1}{B^2}\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_b X_b\right)$, since a constant comes out squared
$= \frac{1}{B^2}\left(\sum_b \operatorname{Var}(X_b) + \sum_{b \ne c} \operatorname{Cov}(X_b, X_c)\right)$, the variance of a sum
$= \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{(1 - \rho)\sigma^2}{B}$, dividing by $B^2$ and collecting the $\rho\sigma^2$ terms

hints.text: Take the $\frac{1}{B}$ out of the variance first.
The variance of a sum is every variance plus every covariance.
Scale, expand the sum, count the terms, tidy up.

feedback.correct: Only the second term shrinks with $B$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pull out the constant, expand, count, then simplify.

byKey.count: You can only count terms once the sum has been expanded into variances and covariances.
byKey.tidy: The tidy form comes last, after counting $B$ variances and $B(B - 1)$ covariances.

explain.text: $\frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{(B - 1)\rho\sigma^2}{B} = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{(1 - \rho)\sigma^2}{B}$. As $B$ grows the second term vanishes and $\rho\sigma^2$ stays. To lower the floor we must lower $\rho$.

screens.title: Two floors
screens.prose: We grew pairs of trees on 200 fresh books of 400 loans and measured both numbers. Bagged trees: $\rho = 0.11$, $\sigma^2 = 0.146$. Trees that see only 2 random features per split: $\rho = 0.04$, $\sigma^2 = 0.175$.

params.yLabel: Variance of the average, in units of $\sigma^2$

state.caption: Bagged trees, $\rho = 0.11$: in units of $\sigma^2$ the floor is 0.11

screens.question: What is the variance floor $\rho\sigma^2$ for the trees that see 2 features per split?

hints.text: The floor is the term that survives large $B$.
Multiply that tree's $\rho$ by its $\sigma^2$.

feedback.correct: Less than half the bagged floor of 0.016.

byKey.bag: That is the bagged trees' floor. Use $\rho = 0.04$ and $\sigma^2 = 0.175$.
byKey.sig: 0.175 is one tree's variance, the value at $B = 1$. The floor multiplies it by $\rho$.
byKey.rho: $\rho$ alone is the floor in units of $\sigma^2$. Multiply by $\sigma^2 = 0.175$.

explain.text: Each restricted tree is noisier, 0.175 against 0.146. But their correlation drops from 0.11 to 0.04, so the floor falls from 0.016 to 0.007. Worse trees, better average.

canvas.caption: Restricted trees, $\rho = 0.04$: the floor drops to 0.04 $\sigma^2$

screens.title: The formula in code
screens.prose: Turn the derivation into a function you can reuse when you size an ensemble.
screens.question: Complete `average_variance(sigma2, rho, B)`: the variance of the average of `B` predictors.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, including the independent case, identical predictors and a single predictor. Each answer is compared with math.isclose. Plain Python is enough.

hints.text: Two terms: one that ignores $B$ and one divided by $B$.
The first term is the floor, $\rho\sigma^2$.
`return rho * sigma2 + (1 - rho) * sigma2 / B`.

feedback.correct: At 100 trees: 0.0174 for bagged trees, 0.0087 for restricted ones.

explain.text: With $B = 1$ the formula gives $\sigma^2$ whatever $\rho$ is: one tree is one tree. At 100 trees the restricted ensemble has half the variance of the bagged one.

screens.title: Random features at each split
screens.prose: A **random forest** is bagging plus one change: at every split, the tree may look at only $m$ features drawn at random. In scikit-learn, `max_features=m`. With $m = 2$ of 8, leverage is often not on offer.

state.caption: Forest with $m = 2$: of 100 roots, 25 split on leverage

screens.question: At the root, what is the chance that leverage is one of the 2 features on offer?

hints.text: Count the pairs of features that leave leverage out.
There are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ pairs; $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ of them miss leverage.

feedback.correct: One root in four can use leverage, and 25 of the 100 did.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the share of the 28 pairs that include leverage.

byKey.one: $1/8$ is the chance with one feature on offer. Two features double it.
byKey.pair: $1/28$ is the chance of one particular pair. Seven pairs contain leverage.
byKey.miss: 0.75 is the chance leverage is left out.

explain.text: Seven of the 28 pairs contain leverage, so $7/28 = 0.25$. When it is on offer it nearly always wins, which is why 25 of the 100 roots use it. The other 75 trees must start elsewhere, so they differ.

screens.title: Choosing $m$
screens.prose: Grow forests of 100 trees on the same 400 loans with each $m$ from 1 to 8, and score each on the 2,000 new loans. scikit-learn's default for a classifier is $m = \sqrt{p}$, rounded down: 2 here.
screens.question: What is the forest with $m = 8$?

options.text: Plain bagging: every split may use every feature
The strongest forest, since it sees the most features
options.why: You expected more choice to help. $m = 8$ has the highest error here, 0.2115 against 0.196.

options.text: A forest of fully random splits
options.why: That is closer to $m = 1$, where each split gets one random feature and no choice.

options.text: An overfitted forest that needs fewer trees
options.why: Its trees are not deeper than the others'. They are just more alike.

hints.text: What does a split choose among when $m = p$?
With all 8 features on offer, nothing random is left inside the trees.
Only the bootstrap rows differ between trees: that is bagging.

feedback.correct: $m = p$ is bagging; smaller $m$ decorrelates the trees.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is random about a tree when $m = 8$.

explain.text: With $m = 8$ only the resample differs between trees, so this is bagging, at 0.2115. The best $m$ here is 2, at 0.196: 1.6 points better. Across 12 books the average gain was 0.7 points: modest and steady.

screens.title: The curve in code
screens.prose: Write the scan. Fix `n_estimators=50` and `random_state=0`, so every $m$ sees the same resamples and the comparison is fair.
screens.question: Complete `rf_test_acc_by_m` so it returns the test accuracy for each `m` in `ms`, rounded to 4 places.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

NAMES = ["leverage", "cover", "margin", "vol", "short", "drawdown", "size", "age"]

def make_loans(seed, n=400):
    """n company loans, 8 features as z-scores across the book.
    y = 1 if the loan defaulted within a year. Leverage matters most;
    the next five matter a little; size and age carry no signal."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, 8))
    z = (-0.3 + 2.5 * X[:, 0]
         + 0.7 * (-X[:, 1] - X[:, 2] + X[:, 3] + X[:, 4] + X[:, 5]))
    y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
    return X, y

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

def rf_test_acc_by_m(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, ms):
    out = []
    for m in ms:
        forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_features=m,
                                        random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
        out.append(round(float(forest.score(X_test, y_test)), 4))
    return out

hints.text: Build the forest with three keyword arguments, then `.fit` it.
`max_features=m` is the only argument that changes inside the loop.
`forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_features=m, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)`.

feedback.correct: With 50 trees on book 9: 0.792 at $m = 1$ and 2, 0.786 at $m = 8$.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Fit a new forest for each `m`, with `n_estimators=50` and `random_state=0`.

explain.text: A forest needs little tuning: $m$ near $\sqrt{p}$, enough trees for the curve to flatten, and sometimes a depth cap. The gaps between $m$ values are small, so tune on validation data, not on the test set.

screens.title: Is the vote a probability?
screens.prose: The forest's `predict_proba` is the share of its trees voting default. A colleague uses it as each loan's probability of default for pricing. Here is how the $m = 2$ forest's votes compare with what happened to 2,000 new loans.
screens.question: What does the table say about using the vote as a probability?

options.text: It is pulled towards 0.5: low votes overstate default and high votes understate it
It is a calibrated probability, since it is a fraction between 0 and 1
options.why: You read a share of trees as a chance. Loans with a mean vote of 0.19 defaulted only 9.6% of the time.

options.text: It is overconfident: it says 0.9 when the truth is nearer 0.5
options.why: Look at the top row: a mean vote of 0.934 against 96% defaulted. The forest is too cautious, not too bold.

options.text: It ranks loans badly, so it is useless
options.why: The ranking is good: the default rate rises in every row. Only the scale is off.

hints.text: Compare the mean vote with the default rate, row by row.
Rows 2 and 3 have votes above the default rate; row 5 has a vote below it.
Votes of 0.19 meet 9.6% defaults; votes of 0.79 meet 86%. The votes are squeezed towards the middle.

feedback.correct: The vote ranks loans well but is not calibrated.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the mean vote with the default rate in each row.

byKey.fine: You read the share of trees as a probability. In the 0.1 to 0.3 row the vote says 0.19 and 9.6% defaulted.

explain.text: Averaging trees that each saw different rows pulls the vote towards the middle. The order is right, the scale is not. Calibrate on held-out loans, as in *Probabilities you can trust*, before pricing with it.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

def rf_vote_fraction(X_train, y_train, x_query, n_estimators):
    forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n_estimators,
                                    random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    x = np.asarray(x_query, dtype=float).reshape(1, -1)   # one row
    votes = [tree.predict(x)[0] for tree in forest.estimators_]
    return round(float(np.mean(votes)), 4)

`tree.predict(x)` returns an array with one class; take `[0]`.
`votes = [tree.predict(x)[0] for tree in forest.estimators_]`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Ask each tree in `forest.estimators_` for its class on `x`, then average.

explain.text: Deep trees have pure leaves, so each tree's probability is 0 or 1 and the forest's `predict_proba` is exactly this vote share. With shallower trees it averages leaf shares instead. Either way it still needs calibrating.

screens.title: The feature that eats the model
screens.prose: A credit desk scores 12,000 loans on 30 features. In its bagged trees, leverage wins every root split, so every tree looks alike. It switches to `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_features="sqrt")`.
screens.question: With $m = \lfloor\sqrt{30}\rfloor = 5$, what share of root splits even have leverage on offer?

widget.label: Share of roots with leverage on offer

hints.text: On the 8-feature book, 2 of 8 gave a chance of $2/8$.
Each feature is equally likely to be among the 5 drawn.

feedback.correct: Five in six trees must start without leverage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A random 5 of 30 features includes any given one with chance $5/30$.

byKey.sqrt: You used $\sqrt{30} = 5.48$ before rounding down. scikit-learn uses 5 features.
byKey.one: $1/30$ is the chance for one feature on offer. Five are on offer.
byKey.miss: That is the share without leverage on offer.

explain.text: $5/30 = 0.167$, so about 33 of the 200 trees can start with leverage. The rest must find structure in the other 29 features, which decorrelates the vote. With defaults like these, 200 shallow-to-deep trees and little tuning, a forest is the desk's standard tabular baseline.

ideas: The average of $B$ predictors with variance $\sigma^2$ and correlation $\rho$ has variance $\rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$; for large $B$ only $\rho\sigma^2$ is left.

A random forest lowers $\rho$ by offering each split only $m$ random features (`max_features`): $\sqrt{p}$ for classification and $p/3$ for regression in the textbooks (scikit-learn's regressor uses all $p$ by default); $m = p$ is plain bagging.
Forests need little tuning, but their vote share ranks well and is not a calibrated probability.

formula.name: Variance of an average of correlated predictors
formula.note: More trees shrink the second term; only lower correlation shrinks the first.

summary.trap: The share of trees voting default is not the probability of default: it is pulled towards 0.5. Calibrate before pricing.

quiz.prose: A colleague fits `RandomForestClassifier(max_features=None)` on 8 features and calls it an improvement on their bagged trees.
quiz.question: How does it differ from `BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier())`?

options.text: Hardly at all: every split sees every feature, so it is bagging
It decorrelates the trees, so it is better
options.why: Decorrelation comes from a small `max_features`. With `None` every split sees all 8.

options.text: Its trees grow deeper
options.why: Both grow deep trees by default. Depth is not the difference.

options.text: It does not resample the rows
options.why: A forest bootstraps the rows by default, exactly as bagging does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is random inside each tree when `max_features=None`.

explain.text: With every feature on offer, only the bootstrap rows differ between trees. That is bagging under another name.

quiz.prose: A forest classifies loans on only 2 features, leverage and cover. scikit-learn's default is $m = \lfloor\sqrt{2}\rfloor = 1$.
quiz.question: What happens at each split?

options.text: The tree must split on one feature picked at random, best threshold or not
It compares both features, as bagging would
options.why: That is $m = 2$. With $m = 1$ there is no comparison to make.

options.text: It always splits on leverage, the stronger feature
options.why: The feature is drawn at random before the split looks at the data.

options.text: It cannot split, since one feature is too few
options.why: One feature is enough to split; the tree just takes the best threshold on it.

feedback.correct: Half the splits use the weaker feature.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $m = 1$, how many features does a split get to choose between?

explain.text: With $m = 1$ the feature at each split is a coin flip, so half the splits use cover even where leverage is far better. With $p = 2$ the choice is only between $m = 1$ and bagging, so check both on validation data.

quiz.prose: On book 9 we grew forests of depth-3 trees. Test accuracy: 0.7815 with $m = 1$, 0.792 with $m = 2$, 0.7775 with $m = 8$.
quiz.question: Why does $m = 1$ fall behind $m = 2$ here?

options.text: Each split is forced onto a random feature, and with only 3 levels the trees rarely reach leverage: high bias
Its trees are too correlated
options.why: $m = 1$ gives the least correlated trees of all. Their problem is that each one is weak.

options.text: It overfits the 400 loans
options.why: Depth-3 trees with random splits fit the data loosely. That is bias, not overfitting.

options.text: It needs fewer trees
options.why: More or fewer trees cannot repair trees that each split on the wrong features.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how good one $m = 1$ tree of depth 3 can be.

explain.text: Lower $m$ lowers $\rho$ but raises each tree's error. At $m = 1$ with shallow trees the second effect wins. The best $m$ sits in between.

quiz.prose: Fifty predictors each have variance 0.04, and any two have correlation 0.3.
quiz.question: What is the variance of their average?

feedback.correct: The floor, 0.012, is almost all of it.

byKey.ind: That is $\sigma^2/B$, which assumes independence. Add the floor $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.012$.

explain.text: $0.3 \times 0.04 = 0.012$ and $0.7 \times 0.04 / 50 = 0.00056$, total 0.01256. Doubling to 100 predictors would save only 0.00028.
